newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Weather continues to plague E.Europe beet.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Weather continues to plague E.Europe beet.

text.p: Sugar beet producing regions in central and eastern Europe continue to suffer from the effects of bad weather over growing areas as a more accurate picture of total production emerges as the harvest gets underway.
The region's two largest producers, Russia and Ukraine, are both forecast to produce less sugar than last year due to adverse weather conditions.

Sugar output in Europe's post-communist nations is widely forecast to be lower this year and was recently estimated by trade house E D & F Man at 8.66 million tonnes white value, down by 289,000 tonnes from the 1995/96 crop year.
UKRAINE--DROUGHT CUTS PRODUCTION
Ukraine, the region's largest producer, continues on course for a lower sugar output after suffering a drought through the summer and cold rains in recent weeks.
"We will get about 26 million tonnes of sugar beets this year," said Leonid Bershtein, a deputy director of the Sugar Research Institute. The last harvest produced 30 million tonnes.
"The recent rains have meant little for our beets. This year the drought had a greater influence," Bershtein said.
Less than 10 percent of all beets sown had been gathered, he said, with the harvest expected to end in November.
Yields for the entire crop would probably be less than 20 tonnes per hectare, compared with 21.9 tonnes last year, and the real sugar content at refineries no more than 12 percent.
"We only have a third of the necessary fertiliser and we have absolutely no herbicides," Bershtein said. "Old equipment means that we lose about 10 percent of the harvest annually."
RUSSIA--WORST CROP IN DECADES
In Russia, the beet harvest is likely to be one of the worst in decades, but industry analysts said high reserves of whites and cheap Ukrainian imports would compensate for low output.

"We still expect the beet harvest to total 17 million tonnes," said Mikhail Sushkov, head of the Rossakhsvyokla sugar beet producers association, adding that rain had slowed work at the beginning of the harvest.

Russia's beet harvest, which is only just starting, could still be affected by bad weather, analysts said. Beet gathering is reported to be proceeding slowly and the quality of the beet harvested so far is under threat.
POLAND--OUTPUT RISING
But the outlook for Poland, the region's third largest producer, is better and this year's output is expected to rise.

Despite a long winter and rainy summer, official estimates put Polish beet output at 15.5 million tonnes, 2.2 million higher than last year, which could translate into a white sugar output of around two million tonnes.
Poland produced nearly 1.6 million tonnes of sugar in 1995.
The first sugar beet test on September 2 showed average sugar content at 13.78 percent, down from 14.34 percent a year ago, but average root weight increased to 732 grammes from 664.
Poland will hold its second and last beet test on October 7 and results are expected after October 20.
CZECH REPUBLIC--DISRUPTION FROM RAINS
Industry sources in the Czech Republic said yields would probably be high compared with previous years, although recent heavy rainfall could disrupt the autumn harvesting.
Czech sugar output is estimated at more than 500,000 tonnes this year after the 460,035 tonnes produced in 1995/96.
"The weather conditions were not as extreme as in other years, except that there was an exceptional amount of rain," said Jiri Janda, director of Prague-based refiner Prazska Cukerni Spolecnost a.s.
"Climatic conditions were favourable, the beet turned out well and it looks like there will be solid yields. Domestic consumption will definitely be covered," he said.
But he cautioned that the final output would still be affected by weather conditions during harvest and field losses could be expected if the rains continued.
HUNGARY--LOW SUGAR CONTENT
Higher beet weights in Hungary are not expected to increase final sugar output to any significant degree.
"The roots were fattened by rains but their sugar content is very low," said a Sugar Industry Association official.
Chairman Andras Angeli said while sugar yields would not be a great deal higher, more sunshine could still boost production.
But according to the National Meteorology Service only a few days of continuous sunshine are forecast for mid-October.
Angeli said Hungary planned to produce 460,000 tonnes of sugar this year, down from 480,000, but beet exports were likely to reach 500,000 tonnes, up from 370,000.
ROMANIA--SHORTAGE OF FUNDS AND FUEL
Romania's beet harvest could be affected by acute shortages of funds and fuel -- and a lack of machinery, inadequate storage and transport delays are expected to cause further delays.
Beet has already been lost on 23,000 hectares of the total 161,950 ha sown due to a harsh winter and late snows, but the remainder is said to be in good condition.

According to the Agriculture Ministry, Romania's 1996 sugar output should reach some 250,000 tonnes after a previous 300,000 and the country might have to import about the same quantity of raw sugar to meet domestic and industry demand.
Many farmers have used only 100 kg of fertiliser per hectare instead of the recommended 160 kg. Others have abandoned growing beet after factories failed to pay them in time last year.
BULGARIA--YIELDS DOWN BY HALF
In Bulgaria, bad weather is expected to reduce sugar yields by almost 50 percent in a crop where the area sown to beet has been slashed to 6,000 hectares from 11,200 last year.
"Bad weather in the spring and plant diseases have spoiled this year's crop," said a Bulgarian Sugar Institute analyst.
He estimated final sugar yield at 23 tonnes per hectare after some 40 tonnes last year.
CROATIA--HARVEST DELAYED
Croatia's beet harvest, which is expected to yield some 880,000 tonnes of sugar, is also being delayed by wet weather.
Sugar content in all of Croatia's main growing areas in the northeast has been affected, although rains in July and August helped root growth and boosted yields, ministry officials said.
"The root needs sunshine and not water any more," said Andrija Kristek, head of the Sugar Beet Institute in Osijek.
"However, since the leaf is well preserved, the beet will not use up sugar to sprout new leaves, so its content could remain at the current 11-13 percent on average."

--Compiled in London newsroom, +44 171 542 8064, with contributions from Irene Marushko in Kiev, Peter Henderson in Moscow, Wojciech Moskwa in Warsaw, Jan Lopatka in Prague, Denes Albert in Budapest, Adrian Dascalu in Bucharest, Elisaveta Konstaninova in Sofia, and Kolumbina Bencevic in Zagreb.
